approach: The research design involves three main components: 1) Clinical Cohort Analysis: Retrospective and prospective analysis of three independent cohorts (melanoma and NSCLC) to assess the association between irAE grades and survival outcomes, correcting for immortal time bias. 2) Microbiome Profiling: Shotgun metagenomics and high-throughput culturomics were performed on fecal samples from patients at baseline and at the onset of ir-colitis to characterize taxonomic shifts and isolate viable bacteria. 3) Functional Validation: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from ir-colitis patients into antibiotic-treated mice to assess effects on tumor growth and inflammation. Specific isolates (P. bifermentans, C. paraputrificum, P. sordellii) were tested in vitro (Caco-2 co-culture for barrier integrity and cytokine expression) and in vivo (oral gavage in DSS colitis and MCA-205 tumor models) to determine direct effects. Cell-free supernatants and heat-killed bacteria were also tested to distinguish live-bacteria-dependent effects from metabolite-mediated effects.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides empirical evidence linking specific gut bacteria (P. bifermentans) to both irAE pathogenesis and enhanced ICI efficacy through distinct mechanisms (barrier disruption vs. metabolite secretion).
contribution_and_limits.limits: The exact nature of the active < 3 kDa metabolite and its precise immune mechanism remain unidentified. The study relies on a limited number of matched longitudinal samples and mouse models that may not fully recapitulate human ir-colitis complexity.

key_findings.conditions: Three independent cohorts of melanoma and NSCLC patients treated with ICI
key_findings.finding: Grade ≥ 2 irAEs are associated with significantly longer overall survival and progression-free survival, even after adjusting for immortal time bias.

key_findings.conditions: Baseline stool samples from melanoma patients analyzed via shotgun metagenomics
key_findings.finding: Patients developing grade ≥ 2 irAEs exhibited lower alpha diversity and enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa including Ruminococcus gnavus and Streptococcus vestibularis compared to those without irAEs.

key_findings.conditions: Stool samples from patients with ir-colitis analyzed via culturomics
key_findings.finding: Paraclostridium bifermentans was isolated and found to be enriched in patients with acute ir-colitis compared to baseline or non-ir-colitis controls.

key_findings.conditions: In vivo mouse models receiving FMT from ir-colitis patients
key_findings.finding: FMT induced surrogate markers of intestinal inflammation (increased Lcn-2 and LPS) and enhanced the anti-tumor efficacy of dual anti-PD-1/CTLA-4 therapy.

key_findings.conditions: In vitro Caco-2 monolayer co-culture with P. bifermentans
key_findings.finding: Live P. bifermentans disrupted epithelial barrier integrity (reduced ZO-1 and Occludin signals) and increased pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α and IL-1β); this effect was not observed with cell-free supernatant.

key_findings.conditions: In vivo murine tumor model with oral gavage of P. bifermentans derivatives
key_findings.finding: Oral administration of P. bifermentans enhanced anti-tumor response to dual ICI; this beneficial effect was retained by cell-free supernatant filtered to < 3 kDa, indicating mediation by a small-molecule metabolite rather than live bacteria.

problem_or_question: The study aims to resolve the mechanism underlying the observed correlation between irAEs and improved ICI efficacy. Specifically, it seeks to determine if specific gut microbial signatures predict irAEs and efficacy, and to identify causal bacterial agents that might drive both inflammation and anti-tumor responses.
research_scope: The study focuses on patients with advanced melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). It investigates the relationship between gut microbiome composition, the development of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), and clinical outcomes (overall survival and progression-free survival). The research combines clinical cohort analysis with shotgun metagenomics and culturomics to identify specific bacterial taxa and their functional roles.
work_summary: This study addresses the paradoxical link between immune-related adverse events (irAEs) and improved efficacy in ICI therapy by dissecting the role of the gut microbiome. Using three independent cohorts totaling 589 patients with melanoma or NSCLC, the authors first validated that grade ≥ 2 irAEs are associated with significantly longer overall survival and progression-free survival, even after adjusting for immortal time bias. They then employed a combined approach of shotgun metagenomics and culturomics on fecal samples collected at baseline and during ir-colitis onset. Metagenomic analysis revealed that patients developing irAEs had lower alpha diversity and enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa such as Ruminococcus gnavus and Streptococcus vestibularis. Culturomics identified Paraclostridium bifermentans as enriched in patients with acute ir-colitis. Functional validation in mice demonstrated that fecal microbiota transplantation from an ir-colitis patient induced subclinical colitis markers and enhanced anti-tumor activity of dual ICI. Specifically, P. bifermentans was shown to disrupt epithelial barrier integrity in vitro and exacerbate colitis in vivo via live bacteria interaction, while its anti-tumor benefit was mediated by a secreted low-molecular-weight metabolite (< 3 kDa). These findings provide a mechanistic link suggesting that specific pro-inflammatory bacteria can simultaneously drive toxicity and enhance therapeutic efficacy.
